title: Best Arm Identification in Generalized Linear Bandits via Hybrid Feedback
claim: Our hybrid method needs fewer queries as problem size grows, and cost-aware allocation cuts acquisition cost across feedback price ratios.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right: log-scale line plot, then stacked bar chart
description: Two plots sit side by side. Panel (a) is a line plot on a log y-axis, with stopping queries from 10^3 to 10^6 against dimension d from 2 to 12. Five methods have colored markers and shaded one-standard-deviation bands: RAGE-GLM in blue triangles, ReTS-GLB in green squares, Random in brown circles, DuelTS-GLB in purple diamonds, and HyTS-GLB in orange circles. HyTS-GLB sits lowest, and RAGE-GLM starts highest. Panel (b) is a stacked bar chart of acquisition cost against reward/dueling cost ratio, from 1/3 to 3. Orange marks the dueling share and blue marks the reward share. Solid bars are standard allocation and hatched bars are cost-aware allocation. Black error bars sit on each bar. A legend above the bars explains the four fill patterns. The orange HyTS-GLB curve and the hatched bars draw the eye first.
caption: Scalability and acquisition cost of hybrid-feedback learning. Results are averaged over 30 independent runs, with shaded regions and error bars indicating one standard deviation.
abstract: We study fixed-confidence best arm identification in generalized linear bandits under a hybrid feedback model: at each round, the learner may query either (i) absolute reward feedback from a single arm or (ii) relative (dueling) feedback from an arm pair, both governed by generalized linear models. We introduce a likelihood-ratio--based confidence sequence that unifies heterogeneous generalized linear observations and yields an explicit ellipsoidal confidence set under a self-concordance assumption. Building on this confidence set, we propose a hybrid Track-and-Stop algorithm that adaptively allocates queries by tracking a minimax-optimal design over a joint action space of arms and pairs. We establish $Î´$-correctness and provide almost-sure asymptotic upper bounds on the stopping time. We further extend the framework to a cost-aware setting that accounts for heterogeneous acquisition costs across feedback modalities. Empirical experiments demonstrate that the proposed algorithms significantly improve sample efficiency over baseline methods.
